titre: The Proof Fit in a Single Arm
accroche: On May 14, 1796, Edward Jenner injects cowpox matter into an eight-year-old child, without knowing why it would work
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 14, 1796, in Berkeley, in the English countryside, the physician Edward Jenner takes a little matter from a lesion on the hand of Sarah Nelmes, a milkmaid with cowpox, a mild disease of cows that can be transmitted to humans through contact with infected udders. Through two small incisions, he introduces it into the arm of James Phipps, an eight-year-old boy, the son of his gardener.

## A Hypothesis Born on the Farms

Jenner is not improvising. For years, the idea has circulated in the English countryside that dairymaids who have caught cowpox from cows never contract smallpox, an otherwise fearsome disease that kills a significant proportion of those infected. The only protection known until then, variolation, consists of deliberately inoculating a little smallpox matter to provoke a milder form of the disease; it is itself risky, with a mortality rate on the order of 1 to 2%.

After the inoculation of May 14, James Phipps develops a slight fever and a passing malaise, then recovers within a few days. On July 1, 1796, Jenner takes the decisive step: he inoculates the boy with genuine smallpox matter, to check whether he is protected. No disease develops. Jenner repeats the experiment on other children in the following months, with the same result every time.

## Practice Before Theory

Jenner cannot explain why it works; the notion of a virus does not yet exist, and it will take nearly a century for the theory of immunity to take shape. He notes an effect, describes it precisely in his publications starting in 1798, and names it after the Latin word *vacca*, the cow: vaccination was born as a word before it was a concept.

The method spreads quickly, carried by its raw effectiveness more than by its scientific justification. As early as 1803, the Spanish Balmis expedition carries orphaned children aboard as living reservoirs of the vaccine, cowpox being transmitted from arm to arm for lack of refrigeration, to bring it to the colonies of the Americas and to the Philippines.

## What Ignorance of the Mechanism Did Not Prevent

The shift lies in this gap between proof and understanding: Jenner builds a complete experimental protocol, hypothesis, test, counter-test, without having any of the notions that would have justified it a priori. A century later, Louis Pasteur takes up the word “vaccination” in homage to Jenner to designate his own work on diseases unrelated to cowpox. The method, generalized and refined, leads to the worldwide eradication of smallpox, officially declared by the World Health Organization on May 8, 1980, to date the only human infectious disease to have disappeared from the planet.

repere.texte: On May 8, 1980, the 33rd World Health Assembly officially declares the global eradication of smallpox, under reference WHA33.3, the only human infectious disease eliminated to date.
repere.source: World Health Organization, WHA33.3 — Declaration of global eradication of smallpox, 1980

carte.punch: In 1796, a trial on an eight-year-old child inaugurates the method that will eradicate smallpox.
carte.idee: In 1796, Edward Jenner inoculates an eight-year-old child with cowpox, then exposes him to smallpox to check that he is protected. He does not know why it works: the theory of immunity will take nearly a century to be born. Generalized and refined, the method leads to the eradication of smallpox.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Account of the global eradication campaign led by the WHO.

quiz.question: Why does Jenner's experiment on James Phipps constitute proof, and not merely an observation?
choix: Because Jenner repeated the inoculation on hundreds of children before publishing
Because he then exposed the boy to smallpox itself, to check for the absence of disease
Because the Royal Society had validated his hypothesis before the experiment began
Because he had observed the responsible microorganism under the microscope
quiz.explication: Jenner does not stop at a presumed protection: he then inoculates the boy with genuine smallpox to verify that no disease develops, which turns a hypothesis into a controlled test. The microscopy of viruses did not yet exist, and no scientific institution had ruled beforehand.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does Jenner take the matter he inoculates into James Phipps on May 14, 1796?
choix: From a pustule on the arm of a patient already recovered from smallpox
From a sample sent by a physician colleague in London
From a cow directly, without going through a human being
From a lesion on the hand of Sarah Nelmes, a milkmaid with cowpox
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Jenner takes the matter from a lesion on the hand of Sarah Nelmes, a milkmaid with cowpox, before inoculating it into young James Phipps.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the mortality rate of variolation, the protection method used before Jenner's?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that variolation, the only protection known before Jenner, remained risky, with a mortality rate on the order of 1 to 2%.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the smallpox vaccine transported to the colonies of the Americas and the Philippines as early as 1803?
choix: By ship, kept in flasks refrigerated with ice
By the Balmis expedition, with orphaned children as living reservoirs
By mail, as a dried powder that could withstand the journey
It was not transported: each colony developed its own vaccine
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For lack of refrigeration, cowpox is transmitted from arm to arm; as early as 1803 the Balmis expedition carries orphaned children aboard as living reservoirs to bring it to the colonies and the Philippines.
